title: Virya Paramita
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna
summary: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna encourages everyone to cultivate patient endurance in the face of challenges, recognizing that joy and enthusiastic energy are always available, even in difficult situations. They emphasize the importance of accepting emotions rather than getting caught up in negative thoughts and reactions, and invite the audience to explore practices such as virya (perfect energy) and Shantideva's teachings on cultivating desire and courage, which can lead to freedom and transformation when done without pretense.

Okay.
I think I just have to look at you straight on here.
Well, I do want to welcome everybody, and thanks for being here tonight.
I really want to welcome the Latona family.
I'm grateful that you're here, but disappointed that we all can't share this time together.
Thank you so much for coming and sharing our practice with us.
We've been talking about the six paramitas for the past few weeks, and the paramita for tonight is virya.
I think it's particularly appropriate for Diane.
Virya is translated as energy and strength and right effort, and Norman Fischer translates it as joyful enthusiasm.
So I think those are perfect words to describe Diane's practice.
She faced her cancer with an energetic embrace of life, and she faced her death with directness and courage.
So I would like to welcome her energy here for the rest of the night.
I want to say, though, that when I mention joyful enthusiasm, I do know that many people don't associate it with these past six months.
We have seen a dramatic rise in anxiety, depression, domestic abuse, addictive drug use, and even teenage pregnancies, among other kinds of conditions.
If we haven't been visited by one of these conditions, we might wonder why not.
I've personally managed to keep trucking along pretty good.
I seem to be doing okay.
But with the recent heightened awareness of our racism and inequity, I do have to ask myself why that is.
Could it be because I'm living a life of relative comfort and privilege?
I'm by no means rich, but I do have a roof over my head, more than enough to eat, and health insurance.
I'm educated and I'm white.
So I do wonder if my own energy and enthusiasm are dependent on these conditions.
If they change, and if I'm hit with a catastrophe, how would I handle it?
Our practice teaches us that joy and enthusiastic energy are always available, even in the midst of suffering or dire situations.
Our founding teacher in Japan, Eihei Dogen, says, when you fall down on the ground, you use the ground to get back up.
What he's saying here is that sometimes we deplete our energy, we make mistakes, or we feel like a failure in life.
Maybe we've violated a precept, or maybe we've forgotten about someone who is suffering.
Or maybe we've experienced some loss and we feel lonely and depressed.
That's understandable.
These are tough times.
But what Dogen is telling us is that we can turn our mistakes or our hardships into our teachers.
We get down or we mess up.
We acknowledge our state.
We make some corrections and attitude adjustments, and then we bounce back up again.
We do that over and over again with effortless joy.
That's what virya is.
And this is not just Dogen.
The Dalai Lama says:
*The most difficult period in one's life is the period of greatest gain in knowledge and experience.
The most difficult period in one's life is the period of greatest gain in knowledge and experience.*
And Joan Halifax, in that same vein, says:
*Catastrophe is the essence of the spiritual path.
A series of breakdowns allowing us to discover the threads that weave all of life into a whole cloth.*
So catastrophe is the essence of the spiritual path.
I do know some of Joan Halifax's story.
Some of you might.
She did have a series of catastrophes that catapulted her eventually on to what she's doing today.
So there's a lot of energy behind that.
Our [unclear: "gas"] and our trials don't have to diminish our energy.
We have a storehouse of it in many forms.
Our current understanding of physics and our Buddhist practice agree that energy is limitless.
The energy we feel is the same energy that gives rise to all the basic elements of the universe.
But when we aren't making use of it skillfully, or we assume that our supply is limited, we stop seeing the possibility of transformation.
We grow exhausted and we can't muster the enthusiasm to pick ourselves up again.
I have been thinking a lot about virya as emotional energy, since we've seen so much of that in the news lately.
I've been watching it play out in both harmful and beneficial ways.
With the video of George Floyd's murder, we broke open 400 years of pent-up oppression and repressed outrage.
In the span of only eight minutes and 46 seconds, rage, horror, shock, and despair, all of that hit the nation.
But despite the emotional turbulence, or probably because of it, many of us do seem to be waking up.
I'm actually very hopeful about a positive change.
It may take a long time, even longer than my lifetime, but I'm okay with that.
In Zen, we talk about second arrows.
I know many of you are familiar with that concept.
A second arrow is what we add on to an already painful situation, something that doesn't need to be there.
The original stimulus or the event that was unavoidable triggers an emotional response, and then our minds take off running.
Maybe we blame, complain, catastrophize, do a little self-shaming.
Also comparing, there's a lot of that.
In our minds, a simple gas pain becomes stomach cancer, or a casual sideways glance can be seen as an impending divorce.
Or maybe an unmasked cough is interpreted as a political statement, and it turns into a conflict.
I've seen this happen.
Trungpa Rinpoche has said that our emotions are like a game we started because we enjoyed them so much.
And Norman, actually I've heard him say that we love our suffering.
Eventually we grew intoxicated and we got addicted to our emotions, even the painful ones.
We play those painful memories over and over in our heads.
Eventually that toxic energy in the body is so predominant that we identify with it.
We become it.
We define ourselves by it, forgetting that these emotions are just more passing phenomena, like clouds in the sky, as we often say in Zen.
But there's also good news about emotional energy and intensity.
There's basic wisdom that's inherent in our emotional life if we can get to the root of it and to the purity of the emotion itself.
Get to the root of it and to the purity of the emotion itself.

To do this, Tibetan practices have us turning our attention to the raw energy that's in the body, the sensations that propel our emotions in the first place, before the thoughts and the projections and the second arrow start to appear.
I'm going to read to you here what the Tibetan teacher Ringu Tulku has to say.
*We need the awareness and courage first to see clearly whatever is there and then to accept and endure it, no matter how negative it may be.
Strong anger, for instance, is a very intense and fierce emotion and is usually experienced as being totally overpowering.
It's not a minor thing but constitutes a real challenge.
If we're able to relax within that kind of feeling, we'll be able to relax within anything.
Once this capacity is acquired, it will not matter how strong our emotions are.
It is even said that the stronger they are, the better.
Yet if we are not skillful enough, we will not be able to apply these subtle methods.*
And his buddy Ponlop Rinpoche adds:
*Even when you work with the most destructive emotions, such as rage, if you can penetrate to its essence, you find tremendous space, energy, and luminosity.*
Wow, rage.
But this may not be easy, and probably not a place to start your practice, especially without the direction of a teacher.
Remember, there are years of personal and collective habit energy behind our feelings, and that's particularly true of the painful ones.
For difficult states and even obsessive thinking that persists and overcomes us, Norman Fischer suggests the practice of patient endurance.
If it feels like we're battling or resisting our minds, we can acknowledge and accept the reality of our thoughts and feelings.
We might try saying to ourselves, this is how it is right now.
And we can name the emotion: this is what anger or fear or whatever the emotion is, this is what it feels like.
This is not as exciting as encountering our demons, but it is grounded and stabilizing, and over time it really does change the mind.
I've used this frequently.
I have this awful insomnia problem, and when I can't sleep at night, I just remember Norman's words and it really helps.
So I recommend it.
Just patient endurance.
Not exciting, but very stable.
We have many other alternative practices to choose from, practices that generate the beneficial energy of virya.
They can act as antidotes to intense and potentially overwhelming emotions.
It may seem surprising, but one is the cultivation of desire.
We do see in the texts where early Buddhists put down and distrusted emotional energy, specifically as it related to desire.
The Buddha, in fact, considered desire as one of the three main poisons, one of the three main causes of our suffering.
But Shantideva, an eighth century Buddhist teacher, had something else to say.
When he described the path to virya, or perfect energy, as they called it, he said one should create desire.
He went on even further and said we should be addicted to desire, like someone, he says, hankering for the pleasure and fruit of love play.
I figured he was a celibate monk, but that's what he said.
Of course, the love play he's talking about is the work specific to a bodhisattva.
And the desire he's talking about is the desire for the good and the wholesome.
We usually start out in practice with a desire for healing and relief from the pain in our own lives.
This is perfectly fine.
This is perfectly natural.
But over time, with practice and the support of the community, a broader aspiration begins to emerge.
We realize that our work of caring and concern goes beyond ourselves, and we vow to include all beings in all places.
This is what deepens our commitment to not just think about the teachings, but to act on them.
This is the desire that ignites our bodhicitta, and the desire that leads us to what Shantideva calls the good and wholesome.
But what do we mean by the good and the wholesome?
This is synonymous with having integrity.
Integrity literally means wholeness, to integrate the many fragmented parts of ourselves.
According to Norman Fischer, integrity means, quote:
*that everything in your life is put together as a whole, body, speech, mind, and activity.
Your relationship to yourself, to others, and to the physical world.*
So, wholeness.
But unfortunately, we often end up dividing ourselves into pieces and acting against ourselves in many ways, diffusing our energy.
We might attest to moral principles, but we don't follow up with right action.
We might spend our days multitasking, involving ourselves in too many projects, but not giving our full attention to the one at hand.
We might be pushing away feelings of loss or inadequacy.
The list is endless, how we diffuse our energy.
But at the root of all this division that leads to exhaustion and burnout is our belief in a self separate from others and from the world.
And zazen is our main antidote to this.
It is our opportunity to notice this fragmentation, accept it, and then just fold it all back into the wholeness.
But facing our demons and saving ourselves from ourselves takes the very energy of courage.
Dale Wright says, I was, what's the name of his book again?
The something of perfection, anyway.
Oh, Chris has it, watch this.
There it is, there's Dale Wright's book.
Thank you, Chris.
The six perfections, which is what we've been studying.
Thank you, Chris.
So Dale Wright says that courage is an essential component of the quest for transformation and is among the most prominent manifestations of energy in a bodhisattva.
So courage, the most prominent manifestation of energy in a bodhisattva.
But in order to be courageous, the first step we have to take is to get intimate with our fear.
We're not trying to annihilate fear.
Fear is a biological necessity designed to protect the organism from harm and loss of life.
Trying to wipe it out is an impossible goal that will set us up for failure.
What we're talking about is cultivating courage and acting in spite of the fear.
It's facing life as it is, knowing that there are risks and we may not succeed.
It's not so much the calculated results that matter, but how openly we face them.
I read an article by a Zen teacher, Louis Richmond, if any of you are familiar with him.
He listed the five great fears in Buddhism that he found in early texts.
Some of you may know these.
I found them pretty interesting.
The first four are fear of death, fear of illness, fear of dementia, and fear of loss of livelihood.
According to the text, the fifth great fear of Buddhism, strangely enough, is the fear of public speaking.
He says that the first four are so obviously great fears that it is curious that fear of public speaking is included with them.
Certainly those who have this fear can report that it is paralyzing.
Certainly those who have this fear can report that it is paralyzing, similar to a panic attack.
He goes on.
He says, one person I know who had this fear said quite calmly that they would prefer to slit their throat rather than speak before an audience.
That's a little extreme.
Four of these fears are mostly unavoidable: death, illness, dementia, and loss of livelihood.
I would categorize them as first-arrow fears.
We don't make them up.
They are the initial painful occurrences that we have little control over.
But I bring these up because I have to confess that two from this list, dementia and public speaking, are up there on my list of fears, particularly as I age.
So although I don't plan on slitting my throat, I do prefer to shrink in the corner when called on to speak.
On some lists, dementia has actually been translated as loss of reputation.
So fear of ridicule or harsh judgment is clearly working at the bottom of this fear, making it a second arrow.
I also read that the fifth fear is a fear of supernatural powers.
Obviously, these things have been translated in different ways.
It's a far cry from loss of livelihood or fear of speaking to fear of supernatural powers.
I don't know, but that's what he said.
So anyway, I've created a self to protect, and I'm subject to all the pitfalls that follow: humiliation, embarrassment, feelings of failure.
This can sometimes lead me to perfectionism, trying too hard to get all the details just right.
After all, in Zen practice, there are plenty of details to screw up.
Or plenty of opportunities to see how the other guy is screwing up.
There are so many masks to wear to defend the self and to keep from exposing that vulnerable underside.
To quote Norman again, he says:
*All our comfort zones are actually quite small, and we consistently protect them.
People are now finding themselves in circumstances that they once felt they had mastery over.*
It's my sense that the folks who have been resistant to or angry about wearing masks are really covering over their loss of control.
They're masking human vulnerability and fragility with defiance in the face of a future that's so unknown.
And it's not just those people.
All of us are used to warding off potential threats, real or imagined, and manipulating events so that they have outcomes to our liking.
But as Buddhists, we're taught that everything is always uncertain.
It takes courage to face this reality.
Everything is impermanent and in constant flux and conditioned by innumerable factors.
So when you think about it, every moment you've experienced today is totally unique, different from every moment you experienced yesterday.
And you really have no idea what will happen tomorrow, or in an hour, or really even in the next minute.
No certainties.
All we have are infinite possibilities.
But if every moment is filled with infinite possibilities, then we have infinite choices.
We can reinforce the burdens and stories of our past, or we can meet the fleeting moment with the joyful enthusiasm of a new birth.
A transformation.
That's about what I have.
I don't know how much time I took.
But I have this little quote that I also like to read.
It's about vulnerability, and it's from Joseph Goldstein.
He says:
*If we can be totally ourselves without any pretense, if we can allow ourselves to feel vulnerable and insecure, then there is a wonderful sense of freedom.
We don't have to protect anything.
Being vulnerable and exposed, even though we've been conditioned to be afraid of that, can actually be wonderful because it is a moment when the armor loosens.*
So thank you everybody for helping me loosen my armor tonight.
And we'll say the chant.

*May our intention equally extend to every being and place* *With the true merit of the Buddha's way* *Beings are numberless, I vow to save them* *Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them* *Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them* *Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it*
I think, Ken, I'd like to send you folks to the breakout room.
I should describe to the [unclear: "tonas"].
Are they here still?
I guess not.
So it's you, [unclear: "Telus"].
Oh, no, yeah, there you are.
You don't have to participate in the breakout room if you don't want to.
What we do is we break up into groups of probably just three, and then we discuss maybe something that's come from the talk.
I do have a question that I'm going to toss out here to everybody, but you can talk about whatever came up for you.
What I want to ask is: what has this Zoom practice been for you in terms of your energy and your enthusiasm for practice?
What is this Zoom experience?
Has it diminished it?
Has it increased it?
And how do you feel about it?
That's just something you can talk about, but really anything is up for grabs.
Ken, maybe you can put us out there.
I think we're okay.
Let's do it for 10 minutes.
So give everybody three minutes each or so in your group to talk, and then Ken will flip us back here together.
